en.greeting: Hi! Today we go further with phrasal verbs: which ones split, three-word verbs like come up with, and some everyday idioms. Let's go step by step.

steps.title: Verbs that split: bring it up, point it out
steps.text: From B1 you know two lists: put it off (splits) and look after her (never splits). Let's add new B2 verbs to the first list.
steps.body:
These **split**: **bring up** (a topic), **point out** (a mistake), **work out** (an answer), **take over** (a project), **turn up** (the volume). A noun can go in the middle or after the small word, but **it, them, me, him, her** must go **in the middle**: *bring it up, point them out*.
Indonesian trap: *jemput saya* puts the person right after the verb, so learners say 'pick up me' ✗. With a verb that splits: **pick me up** ✓.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.text: Sari's flight from Bali lands at 11 p.m. She sends her brother a message.

options: Can you pick up me at the airport?
Can you pick me at the airport up?
Can you pick me up at the airport?
question.explanation: pick up splits, so **me** goes in the middle: *pick me up*. 'pick up me' follows the Indonesian order (*jemput saya*), and *up* can't move to the end of the sentence.

steps.title: Verbs that never split: deal with it
steps.text: Other phrasal verbs never split: the person or thing always goes at the end.
steps.body:
**deal with** = menangani · **go through** = memeriksa satu per satu · **stand for** = singkatan dari · **see to** = mengurus. Always at the end: *deal with **it***, *go through **it***. Not 'deal it with' (Indonesian *menanganinya* has -nya at the end, but English keeps **with**).
**turn up** = arrive (datang, muncul) has **no object**: *She turned up late.*
How to know? A dictionary shows *pick **sb/sth** up* (splits) vs *deal with **sth*** (doesn't). (sb = somebody, sth = something.)

steps.title: Build the sentence
steps.text: A customer has sent an angry complaint about a late delivery. Your colleague asks who will handle it.

question.solution: Our manager will deal with it.
question.prompt: Arrange the words: Manajer kami yang akan menanganinya.
question.explanation: deal with never splits, so **it** goes at the end: *deal with it*. 'deal it with' splits a verb that doesn't split.

steps.title: Three-word phrasal verbs
steps.text: You know look forward to, run out of and get on with from B1. Here are six more. The good news: three-word verbs in this lesson never split.
steps.body:
**come up with** = menemukan ide · **put up with** = tahan dengan · **get away with** = lolos · **catch up with** = menyusul · **keep up with** = tidak ketinggalan · **cut down on** = mengurangi.
The object goes at the very end (*put up with **it***), and after the last word comes a noun or **-ing** (*looking forward to **meeting** you*, not 'to meet').
Don't drop a word: 'She came up a great idea' ✗ → **came up with** ✓.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.text: Dimas was ill and missed two weeks of his English course. Now he's behind the other students.

question.prompt: Complete: He's studying every evening to ___ the rest of the class.
question.explanation: He's behind and wants to reach the others: **catch up with** = menyusul. *put up with* = tahan dengan something annoying, and *come up with* is for ideas.

steps.title: Idioms: don't translate word by word
steps.text: Now idioms: fixed groups of words with a meaning you can't guess from each word.
steps.body: *under the weather* has nothing to do with rain, and *a piece of cake* isn't about food. Learn each idiom as one piece, like a new word. Some have an Indonesian match: **break the ice** = mencairkan suasana (the same picture of ice!), **call it a day** = sudahan dulu, **a piece of cake** = gampang banget.

pairs.en: cost an arm and a leg
hit the nail on the head
the ball is in your court

steps.title: Idioms in real life
steps.text: Here they are in everyday situations. Read the context: it tells you the meaning.
steps.body: The words are **fixed** ('a piece of cakes' ✗); only the verb changes (*broke the ice, costs*). Idioms are **informal**: great in conversation and chats, but **avoid them in formal writing** (a cover letter, a report, an essay), and don't use too many at once.

examples.en: The trainer started with a quiz game to break the ice.
examples.id: Trainernya memulai dengan permainan kuis untuk mencairkan suasana.

examples.en: Sorry, I can't come to futsal tonight. I'm a bit under the weather.
examples.id: Maaf, malam ini saya tidak bisa ikut futsal. Saya agak kurang enak badan.

examples.en: Before we start, let's make sure we're all on the same page.
examples.id: Sebelum mulai, pastikan kita semua sepaham dulu.

examples.en: Renting a villa in Bali in August costs an arm and a leg.
examples.id: Sewa vila di Bali bulan Agustus harganya selangit.

examples.en: We've sent them our offer. Now the ball is in their court.
examples.id: Kami sudah kirim penawaran. Sekarang giliran mereka yang memutuskan.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.text: In a meeting about falling sales, Rina says: "Maybe the price isn't the problem. Maybe our delivery is just too slow." Bu Ani answers: "You've hit the nail on the head!"

options: Rina has made a big mistake.
question.explanation: **hit the nail on the head** = tepat sekali: Rina said exactly the right thing. The idiom is praise, so it isn't about a mistake or about stopping.

steps.title: Quick review
steps.text: Flip through these cards to lock it in.

flashcards.back: Can you pick me up at seven?

flashcards.front: Keluhan itu? Saya yang akan menanganinya.
flashcards.back: That complaint? I'll deal with it.
He turned up an hour late.
We've come up with a solution.

flashcards.front: Saya tidak tahan dengan kemacetan ini.
flashcards.back: I can't put up with this traffic.

steps.title: Cheat sheet
steps.text: Here's everything on one page. Keep it for later.

artifact.title: Cheat sheet · Phrasal verbs & idioms
artifact.intro: Some phrasal verbs split (it in the middle), some never split (it at the end), three-word ones never split. Idioms are fixed and informal.
rows: He turned up late. / Turn it up.
What does it stand for? / I'll see to it.
come up with / put up with / get away with
never split: put up with it
catch up with / keep up with / cut down on
break the ice / a piece of cake
under the weather / on the same page
cost an arm and a leg / hit the nail on the head / call it a day / the ball is in your court
mahal banget / tepat sekali / sudahan dulu / sekarang giliranmu
tips: With a verb that splits, **it / them / me / him / her** go in the middle: *pick me up*, not 'pick up me'.
Three-word verbs never split, and after the last word comes a noun or **-ing**: *look forward to meeting you*, *came up with an idea*.
Idioms are informal: use them in conversation, not in a cover letter, report or essay, and don't overuse them.

examples.en: Can I bring up the parking problem at the meeting?
examples.id: Boleh saya angkat masalah parkir di rapat?

examples.en: Our IT team deals with it every Monday.
examples.id: Tim IT kami menanganinya setiap Senin.

examples.en: We came up with a cheaper plan.
examples.id: Kami menemukan rencana yang lebih murah.

examples.en: I'm looking forward to meeting the new team.
examples.id: Saya tidak sabar bertemu tim baru.

examples.en: The first meeting was a bit awkward, but a funny story broke the ice.
examples.id: Rapat pertamanya agak canggung, tapi cerita lucu mencairkan suasana.

steps.text: Want more practice? These pages explain the same verbs another way, with tests.

id.greeting: Hai! Hari ini kita lanjut dengan phrasal verb: mana yang bisa dipisah, yang tiga kata seperti come up with, dan beberapa idiom sehari-hari. Yuk, langkah demi langkah.

steps.title: Kata kerja yang bisa dipisah: bring it up, point it out
steps.text: Dari B1 kamu sudah tahu dua daftar: put it off (bisa dipisah) dan look after her (tidak pernah dipisah). Sekarang kita tambah kata kerja B2 ke daftar pertama.
steps.body:
Yang ini **bisa dipisah**: **bring up** (topik), **point out** (kesalahan), **work out** (jawaban), **take over** (proyek), **turn up** (volume). Kata benda boleh di tengah atau di belakang kata kecil, tapi **it, them, me, him, her** harus **di tengah**: *bring it up, point them out*.
Jebakan bahasa Indonesia: *jemput saya* menaruh orangnya langsung setelah kata kerja, jadi banyak yang bilang 'pick up me' ✗. Dengan kata kerja yang bisa dipisah: **pick me up** ✓.

steps.title: Giliranmu
steps.text: Pesawat Sari dari Bali mendarat jam 11 malam. Dia mengirim pesan ke kakaknya.

options: Can you pick up me at the airport?
Can you pick me at the airport up?
Can you pick me up at the airport?
question.explanation: pick up bisa dipisah, jadi **me** di tengah: *pick me up*. 'pick up me' mengikuti urutan bahasa Indonesia (*jemput saya*), dan *up* tidak boleh pindah ke akhir kalimat.

steps.title: Kata kerja yang tidak pernah dipisah: deal with it
steps.text: Phrasal verb yang lain tidak pernah dipisah: orang atau bendanya selalu di akhir.
steps.body:
**deal with** = menangani · **go through** = memeriksa satu per satu · **stand for** = singkatan dari · **see to** = mengurus. Selalu di akhir: *deal with **it***, *go through **it***. Bukan 'deal it with' (*menanganinya* punya -nya di akhir, tapi bahasa Inggris tetap memakai **with**).
**turn up** = datang, muncul **tidak punya objek**: *She turned up late.*
Cara tahunya? Kamus menunjukkan *pick **sb/sth** up* (bisa dipisah) vs *deal with **sth*** (tidak). (sb = somebody / seseorang, sth = something / sesuatu.)

steps.title: Susun kalimatnya
steps.text: Seorang pelanggan mengirim keluhan dengan marah soal pengiriman yang terlambat. Rekan kerjamu bertanya siapa yang akan mengurusnya.

question.solution: Our manager will deal with it.
question.prompt: Susun kata-katanya: Manajer kami yang akan menanganinya.
question.explanation: deal with tidak pernah dipisah, jadi **it** di akhir: *deal with it*. 'deal it with' memisahkan kata kerja yang tidak bisa dipisah.

steps.title: Phrasal verb tiga kata
steps.text: Kamu sudah kenal look forward to, run out of dan get on with dari B1. Ini enam lagi. Kabar baiknya: phrasal verb tiga kata di pelajaran ini tidak pernah dipisah.
steps.body:
**come up with** = menemukan ide · **put up with** = tahan dengan · **get away with** = lolos · **catch up with** = menyusul · **keep up with** = tidak ketinggalan · **cut down on** = mengurangi.
Objeknya di paling akhir (*put up with **it***), dan setelah kata terakhirnya datang kata benda atau **-ing** (*looking forward to **meeting** you*, bukan 'to meet').
Jangan buang satu kata pun: 'She came up a great idea' ✗ → **came up with** ✓.

steps.title: Giliranmu
steps.text: Dimas sakit dan tidak ikut kursus bahasa Inggrisnya selama dua minggu. Sekarang dia tertinggal dari siswa lain.

question.prompt: Lengkapi: He's studying every evening to ___ the rest of the class.
question.explanation: Dia tertinggal dan ingin menyusul yang lain: **catch up with** = menyusul. *put up with* = tahan dengan sesuatu yang menyebalkan, dan *come up with* untuk ide.

steps.title: Idiom: jangan terjemahkan kata per kata
steps.text: Sekarang idiom: kelompok kata tetap yang artinya tidak bisa ditebak dari tiap katanya.
steps.body: *under the weather* tidak ada hubungannya dengan hujan, dan *a piece of cake* bukan soal makanan. Hafalkan setiap idiom sebagai satu kesatuan, seperti kosakata baru. Ada yang punya padanan dalam bahasa Indonesia: **break the ice** = mencairkan suasana (gambaran esnya sama!), **call it a day** = sudahan dulu, **a piece of cake** = gampang banget.

pairs.en: cost an arm and a leg
hit the nail on the head
the ball is in your court

steps.title: Idiom dalam kehidupan nyata
steps.text: Ini contohnya dalam situasi sehari-hari. Baca konteksnya: dari situ kamu tahu artinya.
steps.body: Kata-katanya **tetap** ('a piece of cakes' ✗); hanya kata kerjanya yang berubah (*broke the ice, costs*). Idiom itu **informal**: cocok untuk obrolan dan chat, tapi **hindari di tulisan formal** (surat lamaran, laporan, esai), dan jangan pakai terlalu banyak sekaligus.

examples.id: Trainernya memulai dengan permainan kuis untuk mencairkan suasana.

examples.en: Sorry, I can't come to futsal tonight. I'm a bit under the weather.
examples.id: Maaf, malam ini saya tidak bisa ikut futsal. Saya agak kurang enak badan.

examples.en: Before we start, let's make sure we're all on the same page.
examples.id: Sebelum mulai, pastikan kita semua sepaham dulu.

examples.en: Renting a villa in Bali in August costs an arm and a leg.
examples.id: Sewa vila di Bali bulan Agustus harganya selangit.

examples.en: We've sent them our offer. Now the ball is in their court.
examples.id: Kami sudah kirim penawaran. Sekarang giliran mereka yang memutuskan.

steps.title: Giliranmu
steps.text: Dalam rapat soal penjualan yang turun, Rina berkata: "Maybe the price isn't the problem. Maybe our delivery is just too slow." Bu Ani menjawab: "You've hit the nail on the head!"

options: Rina has made a big mistake.
question.explanation: **hit the nail on the head** = tepat sekali: yang dikatakan Rina benar-benar tepat. Idiom ini pujian, jadi bukan tentang kesalahan atau menyuruh berhenti bicara.

steps.title: Ulasan cepat
steps.text: Balik kartu-kartu ini supaya makin nempel.
